draft.title: Costs of microeconomic reform
card: Microeconomic reform can lift efficiency and productivity, but it also has costs. The gains are spread across the economy, while the costs often fall on particular groups.
Jobs

When protection is removed from an industry, such as tariffs on imported cars, firms may close or cut staff. Workers there can lose jobs, and some find it hard to move to new work, especially if they live in a region with few other employers.
Inequality
Reform can widen the gap between winners and losers. Some workers and regions gain from lower prices and new jobs, while others lose income or work.
Time and support
Many benefits take years to appear, but the costs are felt straight away. This makes reform hard to win support for, as the people who lose out may oppose it.
draft.remember: Reform brings gains across the economy, but the costs are felt early by some groups and the benefits come later.

a.q: Why can microeconomic reform be hard to win public support for?
opts: Its costs hit some groups early, but its gains come later
Its gains hit some groups early, but its costs come later
Its costs and gains are both spread evenly across everyone
Its costs fall on the whole economy, but its gains are small
a.why: The costs, such as job losses in a protected industry, are felt quickly by a particular group. The gains take years and are spread widely, so few people feel them early. The reverse order in the second option is wrong, because the card says costs come first.
a.clue: Think about who feels the effects first, and who waits.

b.q: The government removes tariffs on imported clothing. Within a year, a clothing factory in a country town closes, and most of its workers cannot find other work nearby. Which cost of reform does this best show?
opts: Job losses in a formerly protected industry
A gain in efficiency that arrives after many years
A fall in prices for consumers across the economy
A rise in output from the more productive firms
b.why: The tariff protected local clothing firms, and removing it led to a closure and lost jobs for workers who could not easily move. Lower prices and higher efficiency can be real gains of reform, but they are benefits and not the cost shown in this case.
b.clue: Look at what happened to the workers, not to the shoppers.

a.best: Its costs hit some groups early, but its gains come later

b.best: Job losses in a formerly protected industry

problems.detail: Why (a) says the reversed order is 'the second option', but options are shuffled. The reversed option ('Its gains hit some groups early, but its costs come later') is shown fourth, and the second option shown is 'Its costs fall on the whole economy, but its gains are small'. The why should name the option by its wording, not its position.

The stem asks 'Which cost of reform', and only one option is a cost; the other three are benefits. The clue about workers adds to this. A Year 12 student can answer by common sense without applying the card's ideas. The distractors should be other costs or plausible near-misses, such as wider inequality or slow-arriving gains.

proposal.remember: Reform's gains are spread wide and often come later. Its costs can fall early on particular groups.

a.q: Why can microeconomic reform be hard to win public support for?
opts: Its costs hit some groups early, but its gains come later
Its gains hit some groups early, but its costs come later

a.why: The costs, such as job losses in a protected industry, are felt quickly by a particular group. The gains take years and are spread widely, so few people feel them early. The option saying gains come early and costs come later reverses the order on the card.

b.q: After tariffs on clothing are removed, shoppers across Australia pay less for clothes. Workers at a few factories in one region lose their jobs. What does this show about reform?
opts: Its gains are spread widely, but its costs fall on a few
Its costs are spread widely, but its gains go to a few
Its gains are spread evenly, so no group loses out
Its costs fall mainly on consumers through higher prices
b.why: Lower prices reach shoppers across the whole country, while the job losses fall on a small group of workers in one region. The option saying costs are spread widely and gains go to a few reverses this, since here the many gain and the few lose.
b.clue: Compare how many people gain with how many people lose.

b.best: Its gains are spread widely, but its costs fall on a few
